cells.tense: You are here, holding the pen, and the thing you tend is nearly handled.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Take what is actually finished — the part you keep circling — and close it today. Your hands go back on the part still growing, and stay there.
cells.core:
The thing you tend is nearly handled, and you can tell the finished part from the growing part. The finished part can be set down without being called a loss. That is the skill here: attention goes where the thing still needs you, and the rest gets lowered. People can feel it in how you carry what you are working on — the grip goes loose exactly where it should.

So find the piece that is actually complete and tell it so in a way you can hear. Then put your hands back on the part that is not done, and keep them there. Release here is not giving up; it is putting the tool down when the work is finished. The hours the closed thing was holding are free for the next thing that is alive.
cells.sheetLine: Let the finished thing be finished, and keep tending what is not.
cells.verb: tending what grows by learning how it grows
cells.place: where what is finished is let go and what is not is held

cells.tense: You will not have released the thing that is already done, and you are bracing against a future that has not arrived.
cells.act: sense what has not happened yet, with wonder
cells.ask: Sit with one ending that is already here — picture what you hope comes after it. Stay with that picture for a minute, without deciding anything.
cells.core:
The ending already here has not been let go, and the waiting is being pushed forward. You are carrying things past their finish line and reaching for what has not come, both at once, so the hands are full and the room is loud. It looks like care; what it costs is the part that is actually here to tend.

Stay with what has not happened yet instead of steering it. Name the ending you are holding open, imagine what comes after with real curiosity — not a plan, a picture — and feel toward that. Wonder about the next thing is available now, and the finished one is not asking to be carried. The grip gets lighter when you can dream ahead of it.
cells.sheetLine: You are holding the finished past and reaching past the present.
cells.verb: tending what grows by learning how it grows
cells.place: where what is finished is let go and what is not is held

cells.tense: You stood at a beginning already behind you, and the door was not walked through.
cells.act: explore a direction before it has a destination
cells.ask: Try a direction you have been circling. Pick the smallest real move — a patch of ground, a page, a first hour — and take it before you know where it leads.
cells.core:
The beginning is where you are standing, and it is behind you. The garden is fine once it is growing; what is missing is the first small move into something not yet proven. You are waiting on a certainty that nobody gets at the start, and standing still is its own place to be.

Start something you actually want to begin, without the guarantee. Pick a first hour that needs no plan, and do that part, before you can see where it leads. The confidence you are waiting to feel comes after the starting. That is the order this thing grows in, and it grows fine in that order.
cells.sheetLine: You are waiting for certainty that starting does not give first.

cells.tense: The release already happened here, and the telling of it leaves out your hand.
cells.act: govern by knowing what to surrender
cells.ask: Hold the plain fact of what you carried — a role, a duty, a way you kept showing up — with your hand on it, visible. Then set it down and move on.
cells.core:
The thing you tend has changed shape lately, and the change did not come from nowhere. You are the one who let it grow into its next form — you loosened your grip and it moved, and the story you tell has it moving without you. Your hand is missing from the account, and it was there.

Say the part you did. Name what you carried to its end, call yourself the one who carried it, then put it down for good. Naming it does not make it a defeat; it makes it a completion, and completions belong to whoever saw them through. From there, the next thing you tend can start with your hand visible on it.
cells.sheetLine: You carried it to the end. Say so, then put it down.

attempts.check: The two flinch-claims the record does not support: that the person has 'stopped' or 'won't' begin (Too Little) and that 'the future is what they tend' instead of the present (Too Much) — both are extrapolations from the status alone, so I have narrowed each to what is observable in the capacity, not their history. A reader could reasonably say the Too Much cell reads their feeling as theirs alone rather than the shared thinning, so I have kept it in the room, not in their head. The Too Little ask survives being wrong because starting a thing that is mine to start needs no guarantee I have stopped; if I have not, it is still a true and small act. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any that promises what the release will fix — 'and then it will be easier' — so I have cut every promise from the closes. The four asks are four different verbs: let, start, drop, choose.
